description: Five khandas, sunyata and buddha-nature; Arahant and Bodhisattva; kamma, metta and the Five Precepts.
content_html:
The Five Aggregates (Khandas)

Buddhism rejects the idea of a fixed, permanent soul. Instead, what we call a ‘person’ is a constantly changing combination of five factors called the five khandas (Sanskrit: skandhas) or five aggregates. These are:

  • Form (rupa): the physical body and material world, including the five senses and their objects.
  • Feeling (vedana): the pleasant, unpleasant or neutral quality of each experience.
  • Perception (sanna): the ability to recognise and identify objects and experiences.
  • Mental formations (sankhara): volition, intention, habits and mental tendencies—including the kamma-generating actions of mind.
  • Consciousness (vinnana): awareness itself—the knowing quality that registers sense data and mental events.

None of these five aggregates constitutes a permanent self. They are all subject to the Three Marks of Existence: they are impermanent (anicca), they contribute to suffering (dukkha), and none of them alone or together constitutes a fixed self (anatta). The five khandas are interdependent, arising through dependent origination. Theravada Buddhism uses the analysis of the khandas to demonstrate anatta empirically: look carefully at any aspect of what you call ‘yourself’ and you will find only these five shifting, conditioned processes—never a permanent ‘I’.

Key Fact

The five khandas are: form (rupa), feeling (vedana), perception (sanna), mental formations (sankhara) and consciousness (vinnana). Theravada Buddhism uses the khandas to support the doctrine of anatta (no fixed self): because each aggregate is impermanent and conditioned, none of them—alone or together—can be a permanent, independent self.

Mahayana Buddhism extends the Theravada analysis in important ways. The Heart Sutta (Prajnaparamita Hrdaya Sutra) famously declares that ‘form is emptiness, emptiness is form’—a statement of sunyata (emptiness). Sunyata extends anatta beyond the self: not just the person but all phenomena lack inherent, independent existence. Everything exists only through dependent origination.

The Diamond Sutta (Vajracchedika) teaches that no fixed marks or characteristics belong to any phenomenon. Both the Heart and Diamond Suttas use paradox and negation to point beyond conceptual thinking toward direct insight. Alongside sunyata, Mahayana tradition also teaches tathagatagarbha (buddha-nature)—the idea that all sentient beings already have the seed or potential for Buddhahood within them. This teaching stands in creative tension with sunyata: everything may be empty of fixed nature, yet there is a positive capacity for Enlightenment in all beings. Pure Land Buddhism connects tathagatagarbha to the story of Amida Buddha, who vowed to enable all beings to be reborn in the Pure Land as a step toward Buddhahood.

Arahant and Bodhisattva

The ideal of the liberated person differs significantly between Theravada and Mahayana Buddhism. In Theravada, the highest goal is to become an Arahant (Sanskrit: Arhat)—a person who has completely eliminated the three poisons and all craving. An Arahant has walked the full Eightfold Path and at death attains Parinibbana: complete liberation with no further rebirth. The Arahant exemplifies personal liberation through discipline and meditation. In Mahayana, by contrast, the highest ideal is the Bodhisattva—a being who has vowed to attain full Buddhahood for the benefit of all sentient beings.

Santideva’s Bodhicaryavatara (3:6–20) expresses the Bodhisattva aspiration powerfully, vowing to remain in the cycle of existence, taking on the suffering of others, until all beings are liberated. The Bodhisattva deliberately delays their own final liberation, motivated by karuna (compassion) and metta (loving kindness). Pure Land Buddhism speaks of Pure Land as a realm created by Amida Buddha’s compassionate vow, accessible to those who call on his name with sincere faith, and providing ideal conditions for achieving Nibbana.

Kamma, Rebirth and the Middle Way

Kamma (Sanskrit: Karma) is the law of intentional action and its consequences. Every deliberate thought, word and deed plants a seed that will bear fruit in this or a future life. It is important to note that Buddhist kamma is about intention, not just outcome: it is the intention behind an action that determines its kamma-generating quality. Unskilful actions (rooted in Lobha, Dosa or Moha) generate negative kamma; skilful actions generate positive kamma. The result of kamma over many lifetimes is punabbhava (rebirth or rebecoming)—the continuation of the cycle of samsara.

Key Fact

The Five Precepts (pancha sila) are the ethical foundation of lay Buddhist life. They are: (1) to abstain from taking life, (2) to abstain from taking what is not given, (3) to abstain from sexual misconduct, (4) to abstain from false speech, and (5) to abstain from intoxicants. The Karaniya Metta Sutta teaches the practice of universal loving kindness (metta) toward all beings without exception.

Buddhist ethics are grounded in the concept of internalisation of virtue: the goal is not merely outward compliance with rules but the cultivation of inner states—compassion (karuna), loving kindness (metta), equanimity (upekkha) and sympathetic joy (mudita)—that naturally express themselves in skilful action. The Five Precepts (pancha sila) express sila (ethical conduct) in practical form for lay people.

Buddhist ethics use the language of ‘skilful’ (kusala) and ‘unskilful’ (akusala) rather than ‘good’ and ‘evil’. This framing reflects the tradition’s emphasis on intention and consequence: an action is skilful if it is rooted in non-attachment, kindness and wisdom, and unskilful if it arises from the three poisons (Lobha, Dosa, Moha). Skilful actions reduce suffering and generate positive kamma; unskilful actions increase suffering and generate negative kamma.

The Middle Way is not just a guideline for the physical lifestyle of practitioners (avoiding extreme asceticism and indulgence); it also applies to moral conduct. Santideva’s Bodhicaryavatara (3:6–20) presents the Bodhisattva’s ethical ideal as balancing compassion for others with the wisdom to act effectively. Karuna and panna must work together: compassion without wisdom may cause harm; wisdom without compassion becomes cold. The Six Perfections (paramitas)—generosity, ethics, patience, energy, meditation and wisdom—express this balance. These are the Mahayana elaboration of the ethical dimension of the Buddhist path, cultivated over many lives by the Bodhisattva on the way to full Buddhahood.
exam_tip_html: When explaining the difference between Theravada and Mahayana, do not reduce it to ‘Theravada is selfish, Mahayana is compassionate.’ Examiners expect you to use accurate terms: the Theravada ideal is the Arahant (individual liberation); the Mahayana ideal is the Bodhisattva (liberation for all beings). For a 15-mark ‘Discuss’ question comparing Arahant and Bodhisattva ideals, use named sources—Santideva’s Bodhicaryavatara (3:6–20) for the Bodhisattva vow and the Karaniya Metta Sutta for the teaching on metta. Accurate spelling of ‘Bodhisattva’, ‘Tathagatagarbha’, ‘Pancha Sila’, ‘Karuna’ and ‘Paramitas’ is rewarded in extended responses. Never confuse kamma with fate: in Buddhism, kamma is the result of intentional action, not predestination.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • What we call ‘a person’ is a combination of five aggregates (khandas): form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness; none of these constitutes a permanent self, supporting the doctrine of anatta; Mahayana extends this with sunyata (all phenomena lack inherent existence) alongside tathagatagarbha (all beings have buddha-nature).
  • Theravada’s highest ideal is the Arahant (fully liberated individual); Mahayana’s is the Bodhisattva (who seeks Buddhahood for all beings through compassion); Pure Land Buddhism offers the path via Amida Buddha’s vow and rebirth in the Pure Land.
  • Kamma (intentional action) shapes rebirth; ethical life is grounded in the Five Precepts (pancha sila), loving kindness (metta—Karaniya Metta Sutta) and compassion (karuna); the Middle Way and Six Perfections (paramitas) balance wisdom with compassionate action.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by 'pancha sila' in Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks: The Five Precepts — the basic ethical code for lay Buddhists (accept any equivalent wording that identifies pancha sila as five ethical guidelines). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between the Arahant and the Bodhisattva ideals in Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks: The Arahant is the Theravada ideal: a fully liberated individual who has eliminated the three poisons and will not be reborn. The Bodhisattva is the Mahayana ideal: a being who seeks Buddhahood for the benefit of all sentient beings, motivated by compassion, delaying final liberation. 1 mark: identifying one ideal correctly. 2 marks: describing both with the key distinction (individual vs universal liberation). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline how kamma shapes a Buddhist's understanding of rebirth.
practice_questions.marks:
Creditworthy points (any 3):
• Kamma is the law of intentional action and consequence: every deliberate action generates kamma.
• Unskilful actions (rooted in the three poisons) generate negative kamma; skilful actions generate positive kamma.
• The result of accumulated kamma is punabbhava — rebirth or rebecoming in a new existence.
• The cycle of rebirth (samsara) continues until the three poisons are extinguished through following the Eightfold Path.
[3 marks, 1 per valid point with brief explanation]

practice_questions.text:
Explain the significance of the five khandas for the Buddhist understanding of the self.
Refer to Buddhist teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The five khandas (form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness) are what constitute a 'person'; none is a permanent self.
• Theravada Buddhism uses the khandas to support anatta (no fixed self): each aggregate is impermanent (anicca) and subject to suffering (dukkha), so none can constitute a permanent 'I'.
• The Heart Sutta (Mahayana) extends this via sunyata: 'form is emptiness, emptiness is form' — all five aggregates lack inherent existence.
• The Diamond Sutta reinforces that no fixed characteristics belong to any phenomenon, including the person.
• The practical significance: if the person is not a fixed self, then the clinging to a permanent 'I' (the root of tanha) can be recognised as based on a delusion, making liberation logically possible.
• Mahayana adds tathagatagarbha: within these shifting aggregates is the potential for Buddhahood, balancing emptiness with a positive capacity for Enlightenment.
Mastering: all five khandas listed with their significance for anatta, Theravada and Mahayana treated distinctly, named sources used, significance explained.
Secure: the khandas and their link to anatta explained with at least one named source.
Developing: basic description of the khandas with limited explanation of their significance.
Emerging: a simple mention of the khandas without connecting them to anatta or the self. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'The Bodhisattva ideal is more important for Buddhists today than the Arahant ideal.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The Bodhisattva ideal, expressed in Santideva's Bodhicaryavatara (3:6–20), combines personal spiritual practice with universal compassion, making it highly relevant to the social and ethical concerns of modern life.
• In a globalised, interconnected world, the Bodhisattva vow to work for the liberation of all beings resonates with contemporary values of social justice and environmental care.
• The Mahayana tradition is numerically dominant worldwide (East Asia, Tibet); for the majority of Buddhists, the Bodhisattva ideal is the living norm of practice.
• Pure Land Buddhism (an extremely popular Mahayana school) makes the Bodhisattva path accessible to ordinary lay people through trust in Amida Buddha's compassionate vow.

Arguments against or offering a different emphasis:
• The Arahant ideal remains the living standard in Theravada countries (Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand), which have large and vibrant Buddhist populations. Claiming the Bodhisattva ideal is 'more important' overlooks the lived reality of Theravada communities.
• The Arahant ideal emphasises personal discipline, meditation and inner transformation — these are timeless and do not depend on cultural context. Many argue that if each individual achieved liberation, the collective benefit would be the same.
• Both ideals share the same basis: the Eightfold Path, the Three Jewels and the Four Noble Truths. The distinction between Arahant and Bodhisattva is one of emphasis and scope, not fundamental doctrine.
• The Karaniya Metta Sutta, a Theravada text, already teaches universal loving kindness (metta) to all beings — suggesting that the Theravada tradition also contains the compassionate motivation associated with the Bodhisattva ideal.

Mastering: both sides fully developed with named sources (Santideva's Bodhicaryavatara 3:6–20, Karaniya Metta Sutta), Theravada/Mahayana distinction accurately maintained, explicit weighing and a justified conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered with at least one named source and a clear conclusion.
Developing: some argument on each side with limited sources.
Emerging: one-sided or superficial response with no sources. [15 marks, SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the meaning and importance of metta (loving kindness) in Buddhist ethics.
practice_questions.marks:
Creditworthy points (any 3 from the following):
• Metta means loving kindness or benevolence — the wish for all beings to be happy without exception.
• The Karaniya Metta Sutta teaches the practice of metta as a meditation, cultivating goodwill toward all sentient beings including enemies.
• Metta is one of the four brahmaviharas (divine abodes), alongside karuna (compassion), mudita (sympathetic joy) and upekkha (equanimity); it is central to Buddhist ethics because it generates the positive motivation that underpins all skilful action.
[3 marks, 1 per valid point with brief explanation]

The Buddhist word for intentional action that generates consequences affecting future lives is _____.

right: Theravada ideal: a fully liberated individual who will not be reborn
Mahayana ideal: seeks Buddhahood for the benefit of all beings

flashcard_questions.q: Why do the five khandas support the doctrine of anatta?
flashcard_questions.a: None of the five aggregates is permanent or independent, so none constitutes a fixed self.

flashcard_questions.q: What does sunyata mean in Mahayana Buddhism?
flashcard_questions.a: Emptiness — all phenomena lack inherent, independent existence.
Buddha-nature — the inherent potential for Buddhahood present in all sentient beings.
A Theravada ideal: a fully liberated individual who has eliminated the three poisons and will not be reborn.
A Mahayana ideal: one who vows to attain Buddhahood for the benefit of all sentient beings.

flashcard_questions.q: Which text expresses the Bodhisattva vow to take on others' suffering?

flashcard_questions.a: Loving kindness — the wish for all beings to be happy without exception.

flashcard_questions.q: Which sutta teaches the cultivation of universal loving kindness?
What are the Five Precepts (pancha sila)?
flashcard_questions.a: Abstain from: taking life, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and intoxicants.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the collective term for the six virtues a Bodhisattva cultivates over many lifetimes?

flashcard_questions.a: Compassion — the heartfelt wish to relieve the suffering of others.

glossary_terms.definition: The five aggregates or groups that make up what is mistakenly thought of as a permanent self: form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness.
The Mahayana Buddhist concept that all phenomena lack inherent, independent existence; they are 'empty' of a fixed nature and exist only through dependent origination.
The Mahayana teaching that all sentient beings have the inherent potential to become a Buddha; also called buddha-nature.
The Theravada Buddhist ideal of a fully liberated individual who has eliminated all the three poisons and will not be reborn after death.
A Mahayana Buddhist ideal: a being who seeks to attain full Buddhahood not just for themselves but for the sake of all sentient beings, motivated by universal compassion.
In Mahayana Buddhism, the realm created by Amida Buddha's compassionate vow, where beings can be reborn to practise the Dharma and attain Enlightenment more easily.
Intentional action (physical, verbal or mental) that generates consequences; the Buddhist law of moral cause and effect that shapes future experience and rebirth.
The Buddhist concept of rebirth into a new existence after death; the cycle continues until the three poisons are extinguished and Nibbana is attained.
Compassion; the heartfelt wish to relieve the suffering of others; one of the central ethical virtues in Buddhism.
Loving kindness or benevolence; the wish for all beings to be happy; cultivated through the metta bhavana meditation practice.
The basic ethical code for lay Buddhists, covering non-harming, non-stealing, non-misconduct, truthful speech and abstinence from intoxicants.
